title: Insulin Delivery Devices Market Size, Share & Forecast 2026-2032

market_overview.summary: Published insulin delivery device estimates for 2024 run from $10.11 billion to about $35.6 billion — a 3.52x spread — and the stated CAGRs run from 5.17% to 15.3% in the wrong direction, with the lowest base claiming the highest growth. We publish Global Market Insights' October 2026 series, the only one in the set whose own segment and regional tables sum exactly to its own total: $21.90 billion in 2026 rising to $34.56 billion by 2032 at 7.9%. This market has unusually good denominators, and they expose two things. First, a taxonomy failure: Insulet's $2.7 billion of Omnipod revenue is almost entirely disposable pods, a consumable, against a global pump-consumables segment of $900 million — a factor of three. Second, and more useful than any dollar figure: Insulet, Tandem and Beta Bionics publish patient counts alongside revenue, so revenue per patient is directly checkable at $4,500, roughly $3,383 and $2,865 a year. Inverting the published pump-side total of $7.40 billion gives a global pump population of 1.6 to 2.6 million people — under half of one percent of the 589 million adults the IDF counts as living with diabetes, 252 million of whom do not know it.
key_trends: Patch pumps are taking the category: Insulet grew Omnipod revenue 31.6% to $2.7 billion in FY2025 and passed 600,000 estimated active users globally, ranking first in new customer starts in both the United States and Europe

Type 2 diabetes, not type 1, is where the pump growth now comes from, which is what turns a 1.6-to-2.6-million-patient market into a plausible multi-million one — and it is the explicit driver Insulet cites for its FY2025 outperformance

The pharmacy channel is replacing durable medical equipment: Beta Bionics' pharmacy sales rose 295% in the fourth quarter of 2025 and the pharmacy share of its new patient starts went from a high single-digit percentage to the high twenties in one year

That channel shift breaks the revenue series. Tandem's 2026 guidance of $1.065-1.085 billion includes $85-95 million of headwind purely from moving United States customers to pay-as-you-go pricing with no upfront pump reimbursement, while it guides pump shipments up 10-11%

Automated insulin delivery is now the product, not the pump: Medtronic's fiscal 2025 Diabetes growth of 10.7% is attributed to MiniMed 780G installed base and CGM attachment rates, and it has filed 510(k)s for an interoperable pump and algorithm to pair with an Abbott-based sensor

Structural separation is under way at the largest incumbent: Medtronic announced its intent to separate the Diabetes business into a standalone public company within 18 months, which will for the first time put a pump-and-CGM pure play of that scale on public record
market_overview.adoption_level: Pens and syringes near-universal where insulin is available; pumps under 0.5% of people with diabetes

drivers: Type 2 diabetes adoption of pump therapy, which Insulet names as the main driver of its 31.6% FY2025 Omnipod growth and which is the only mechanism that can move pump penetration above the current 0.3-0.4% of people with diabetes

Automated insulin delivery algorithms paired with continuous glucose monitoring, now the actual product being bought: Medtronic cites MiniMed 780G installed base and CGM attachment rates as its fiscal 2025 growth drivers
Pharmacy-channel distribution, which removes the durable medical equipment paperwork barrier — Beta Bionics' pharmacy sales grew 295% in Q4 2025 and Tandem is migrating its whole United States base
A very large and still-growing population: the IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th edition counts 589 million adults aged 20-79 with diabetes in 2025, projected to reach 853 million by 2050
Geographic expansion of patch pumps into markets with no prior pump infrastructure: Insulet launched Omnipod 5 in nine new markets during 2025 and grew international revenue 44.1%

Interoperability mandates and filings that unbundle the pump from the sensor, including Medtronic's 510(k) submissions for an interoperable pump and algorithm, which widens the addressable base for every algorithm vendor
restraints: The commodity half of the market barely grows. Pen needles, syringes and testing strips are about $5.00 billion of the published 2025 total and compound at 2% to 4.5% on the same publisher's own figures, which caps any blended rate

Pump therapy reaches under half of one percent of people with diabetes, and 252 million of the 589 million adults with diabetes are undiagnosed, so the near-term constraint is diagnosis and insulin access rather than device choice

Reimbursement model change suppresses reported revenue: Tandem's own 2026 guidance carries $85-95 million of headwind from pay-as-you-go pricing while patient volumes rise, so the dollar series understates the patient series
Device revenue is about $34 per person with diabetes per year worldwide, which is what happens when most insulin outside high-income markets is delivered by a disposable syringe

Quality-system and regulatory exposure at the smaller vendors, including the FDA warning letter Beta Bionics addressed on its fourth-quarter 2025 call, which for a single-product company is an existential rather than an operational risk
Pricing pressure from channel conversion: pharmacy distribution removes the upfront pump payment that funded the capital, so vendors take the margin over a longer recurring stream
opportunities: Type 2 pump penetration, which is the single largest identifiable step change available: moving from 0.3-0.4% of the diabetic population to 1% would roughly triple the pump side of the market
Markets with no existing pump base, where Insulet's nine new Omnipod 5 launches in 2025 produced 44.1% international revenue growth off a small base
Algorithm and software licensing decoupled from hardware, enabled by interoperability filings of the kind Medtronic has made for a pump and algorithm pairing with an Abbott-based sensor
The Medtronic Diabetes separation, which will create a listed pump-and-CGM company of scale and for the first time put a pump-attributable revenue line on public record

Consumables economics on an installed base: a 3-day disposable pod generates $4,500 a year per user on Insulet's disclosed figures, which is a recurring revenue profile closer to pharmaceuticals than to capital equipment
challenges: The published taxonomy cannot hold its own largest participant. Insulet's $2.7 billion of disposable pod revenue is three times the $900 million global pump-consumables segment, and classifying pods as tubeless pumps instead makes one company 90% of that segment

Five disclosures consume 93% of the published pump side of the market: Insulet, Tandem, Beta Bionics, Medtronic Diabetes and Ypsomed's former Diabetes Care business leave about $495 million for Roche, Sequel, Medtrum, Equil, SOOIL and every Chinese and Indian vendor combined

A single blended CAGR describes nobody. Companies in this market grew 10.7% to 54% in FY2025 while the commodity segments grow at 2% to 4.5%, and the published 7.9% is the average of two unrelated businesses
Published CAGRs run inversely to published bases — the lowest base claims 15.3% and the highest claims 5.17% — which is the signature of rates reverse-engineered to hit a predetermined endpoint

One publisher's page carries content about asthma inhalers, COPD, cystic fibrosis and nasal congestion inside an insulin delivery report, which means at least one estimate in the public record was not assembled from insulin device data at all
Revenue is about to stop tracking adoption as the pharmacy transition proceeds, so analysts measuring this market in dollars will diverge from the clinical reality measured in patients

regulatory_landscape: Insulin pumps are Class II devices in the United States and have historically cleared through the FDA 510(k) pathway. Since 2019 FDA has recognised an Alternate Controller Enabled infusion pump pathway — the interoperable pump, or ACE pump — which permits a pump to be cleared for use with a compatible controller and algorithm from a different manufacturer. Medtronic submitted 510(k) applications under that framework for an interoperable pump and algorithm during fiscal 2025.

Automated insulin delivery requires three separate authorisations that must then be shown to work together: the pump as an ACE pump, the sensor as an integrated continuous glucose monitor (iCGM), and the dosing algorithm as interoperable automated glycaemic controller software. A system is only marketable when all three clearances exist and compatibility is demonstrated, which is why Medtronic's Simplera Sync approval for use with MiniMed 780G was reported as a discrete regulatory event.

Channel classification determines reimbursement. Pumps supplied as durable medical equipment are paid under Medicare Part B with upfront reimbursement for the device; pumps supplied through the pharmacy channel are paid under Part D or commercial pharmacy benefit as a recurring supply, with no upfront payment. That distinction, not any clinical change, is what produces the $85-95 million revenue headwind in Tandem's 2026 guidance.

FDA quality system regulation at 21 CFR part 820 — now converging on ISO 13485 under the Quality Management System Regulation — is the enforcement surface for this category, and warning letters are a live risk for single-product companies: Beta Bionics addressed one tied to quality-system observations on its fourth-quarter 2025 earnings call.

EU Medical Device Regulation 2017/745 governs pumps, pens and infusion sets placed on the EU market, with notified-body conformity assessment and post-market clinical follow-up; insulin pens supplied as part of a drug-device combination are additionally assessed under the medicinal product framework, which is one reason pen hardware revenue is never reported separately.

Pen needles, insulin syringes and infusion sets are regulated as Class II sharps with 510(k) obligations and, in the United States, are additionally subject to the Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act's requirements on sharps injury protection — a commodity regulatory regime quite unlike the pump pathway, which is part of why a single market definition spanning both is unstable.

research_methodology.data_validation: The 2026 base is Global Market Insights' own published 2026 figure of $21.90 billion, unaltered; the 2032 endpoint is derived by compounding it at GMI's own stated 7.9% rate and is labelled as interpolation. The internal check is that the implied rate between our endpoints is 7.90%, identical to the stated rate. GMI was chosen because it is the only source in the set that is internally consistent — its 2025 product segments sum exactly to its $20.00 billion total, and so does its 2025 regional table, which no other source here can demonstrate — because it is the most recently published with a dated base year, and because its explicit taxonomy is what made the checks below possible at all. Five grounding tests were run against FY2025 reported revenue and the patient counts companies publish alongside it. First, a taxonomy test: Insulet's $2.7 billion of Omnipod revenue is almost entirely disposable pods, which is a consumable, and that is 3.0 times GMI's entire global pump-consumables segment of $900 million; reclassifying pods as tubeless pumps instead makes Insulet 90% of that $3.00 billion segment, leaving $300 million for Ypsomed, Medtrum, Equil, Sequel and every other patch-pump vendor. Second, a containment test: GMI's pump-attributable total for 2025 is $6.50 billion of pumps plus $0.90 billion of pump consumables, or $7.40 billion. Insulet, Tandem and Beta Bionics together disclose $3,849 million, which is 52.0% of it, and none of the three is the global installed-base leader. Adding Medtronic Diabetes at $2,755 million and Ypsomed's former Diabetes Care segment at about $301 million takes five disclosures to $6,905 million, or 93.3%, leaving about $495 million for Roche, Sequel, Medtrum, Equil, SOOIL, every third-party infusion set and every Chinese and Indian vendor. The Medtronic figure includes continuous glucose monitoring revenue that GMI does not count in this market, so it is an upper bound rather than a pump figure, and the pure-play subtotal carries the finding on its own. Third, a revenue-per-patient test, possible because three companies publish both numbers: Insulet $2,700 million over more than 600,000 active users is $4,500 per user per year; Beta Bionics $100.3 million over exactly 35,011 users is $2,865; Tandem $1,015 million over more than 300,000 United States supply-ordering customers is about $3,383 before counting international customers. Because the user counts are floors, these are upper bounds. Fourth, inverting the published total: $7.40 billion divided by $4,500 gives 1.64 million pump users worldwide and divided by $2,865 gives 2.58 million, so GMI's pump side implies a global pump population of roughly 1.6 to 2.6 million — a statement a clinician can check, unlike the dollar figure. Fifth, against the population denominator: $20.00 billion over the IDF's 589 million adults with diabetes is $34 per person per year, and 1.6 to 2.6 million pump users is 0.27% to 0.44% of that population, 252 million of whom are undiagnosed. Finally, the blended rate was tested against company growth: Beta Bionics grew 54%, Insulet 31.6%, Tandem 12% and Medtronic Diabetes 10.7% in FY2025, while GMI's own syringe, strip and pen-needle segments compound at 2% to 4.5%, so the published 7.9% is the average of two unrelated businesses and describes neither. These are scope and plausibility tests, not market estimates. They do not establish the correct figure for any segment. Regional and country splits are published as empty arrays because the only source offering them presents no method, and no vendor market share is published because none is disclosed and the disclosures that exist are not comparable: Insulet's revenue is consumables, Medtronic's includes CGM, and Tandem's is being restructured by a pricing-model change that reduces reported revenue while patient volume rises.

faqs.question: How large is the insulin delivery devices market?
faqs.answer: We publish $21.90 billion for 2026, rising to $34.56 billion by 2032 at 7.9%, from Global Market Insights' October 2026 series. Published 2024 estimates run from $10.11 billion to about $35.6 billion — a 3.52x spread — and the stated CAGRs run from 5.17% to 15.3%, inversely to the bases, which is the signature of rates reverse-engineered to hit a predetermined endpoint. The more useful framing is per person: $20.00 billion for 2025 across the 589 million adults the IDF counts as living with diabetes is about $34 a year each.

faqs.question: How many people worldwide use an insulin pump?
faqs.answer: Roughly 1.6 to 2.6 million, on our arithmetic, and this is the one number in the market you can genuinely check. Insulet, Tandem and Beta Bionics publish revenue and patient counts in the same releases: $4,500 per Omnipod user per year across more than 600,000 users, about $3,383 per Tandem supply-ordering customer, and $2,865 per Beta Bionics user across exactly 35,011. Dividing the published pump-side total of $7.40 billion by those rates gives 1.6 to 2.6 million people — under half of one percent of adults with diabetes.

faqs.question: Does the published market definition hold up?
faqs.answer: Not at the consumables boundary. Insulet sells disposable pods, not a durable pump — the controller is an app — so essentially all of its $2.7 billion of Omnipod revenue is a consumable. One publisher's entire global pump-consumables segment is $900 million. That is a factor of three. The only alternative is to classify pods as tubeless pumps, which makes Insulet 90% of a $3.00 billion segment and leaves $300 million for every other patch-pump vendor on earth. The taxonomy has one coherent place to put the market's fastest-growing company and it does not fit there either.

faqs.question: Does disclosed vendor revenue exceed the published pump market?
faqs.answer: It fills it. The published pump side for 2025 is $6.50 billion of pumps plus $0.90 billion of pump consumables, $7.40 billion in all. Insulet, Tandem and Beta Bionics disclose $3,849 million between them — 52% — and none of the three has the largest installed base. Add Medtronic Diabetes and Ypsomed's former Diabetes Care segment and five disclosures account for 93.3%, leaving about $495 million for Roche Accu-Chek, Sequel, Medtrum, Equil, SOOIL, third-party infusion sets and every Chinese and Indian manufacturer. Medtronic's figure includes CGM, so treat it as an upper bound — but the three pure-plays carry the point unaided.

faqs.question: Why is a single CAGR misleading here?
faqs.answer: Because the market is two businesses glued together. Pen needles, syringes and testing strips are about $5.00 billion of the 2025 total and compound at 2% to 4.5% on the same publisher's own figures. Meanwhile Beta Bionics grew 54% in FY2025, Insulet 31.6%, Tandem 12% and Medtronic Diabetes 10.7%. The published 7.9% sits between them and describes no company in the market. Apply it to either half and you will be wrong in opposite directions.

faqs.question: Why will reported revenue stop tracking adoption?
faqs.answer: Because the channel is changing. Pumps sold as durable medical equipment are reimbursed upfront; pumps supplied through the pharmacy channel are paid as a recurring supply with no upfront device payment. Tandem's 2026 guidance of $1.065-1.085 billion includes $85-95 million of headwind purely from that shift, while it guides United States pump shipments up 10-11%. Beta Bionics shows the same migration: pharmacy sales up 295% in the fourth quarter and the pharmacy share of new starts going from high single digits to the high twenties in one year. Revenue down, patients up.

faqs.question: Which company leads insulin delivery, and what share does it hold?
faqs.answer: Medtronic holds the largest installed pump base globally and Insulet has the largest and fastest-growing disclosed revenue at $2.7 billion. No share is disclosed for anyone and we assign none, because the disclosures are not comparable: Insulet's revenue is consumables, Medtronic's bundles CGM, Tandem's is being suppressed by a pricing-model change, and the pen segment — the single largest part of the published market at about 38% — has no disclosed revenue anywhere, because Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly embed pen hardware in the insulin price.

Tandem's 2026 guidance includes $85-95 million of headwind from pay-as-you-go pharmacy pricing while it guides pump shipments up 10-11% — revenue and patients diverging
market_context: Insulin delivery is two markets filed under one heading, and the filing error is what produces a 3.5x spread. One of them is a commodity: pen needles, insulin syringes and test strips, about $5.00 billion a year on one publisher's figures, compounding at 2% to 4.5%, sold through pharmacy and retail at low unit prices into every country that has insulin at all. The other is automated insulin delivery: pumps, patch pods, infusion sets and the algorithms that run them, about $7.40 billion, whose vendors grew between 10.7% and 54% in FY2025 and whose patient population is on our arithmetic between 1.6 and 2.6 million people. The first market is defined by insulin access; the second by reimbursement, diagnosis and clinical inertia. They share a word and nothing else. The scale of the gap between them is best seen through the population: the IDF counts 589 million adults living with diabetes, 252 million of whom do not know it, which puts total device spend at about $34 per person with diabetes per year and pump penetration at under half of one percent. Everything that gets written about this market — the algorithms, the interoperability filings, the patch-pump launches, the type 2 expansion — concerns that fraction of a percent. And the supplier structure makes the larger half unauditable: Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly supply most of the world's pens with the hardware cost embedded in the insulin price, so the biggest single segment of the published market, roughly 38% of it, has no disclosed revenue line anywhere on earth.
forecast_analysis: Our 7.9% is Global Market Insights' own rate on its own base, and the series reproduces its stated rate exactly. The problem is not the arithmetic, it is that the rate is a weighted average of two businesses that no operator experiences together. The pump side compounds at the rate its vendors actually posted in FY2025 — Beta Bionics 54%, Insulet 31.6%, Tandem 12%, Medtronic Diabetes 10.7% — and the commodity side at 2% to 4.5% on the same publisher's own segment figures. A reader forecasting pumps at 7.9% will understate by half; a reader forecasting pen needles at 7.9% will overstate by double. The structural question that determines which way the blend drifts is type 2 adoption, which Insulet names as the main driver of its outperformance. Moving pump penetration from 0.3-0.4% of the diabetic population to 1% would roughly triple the pump side and would shift the blended rate upward by several points on its own. Against that, two forces suppress the measured series. The first is the pharmacy channel: pumps paid as a recurring supply rather than reimbursed upfront generate less revenue per new patient in year one, and Tandem has quantified that at $85-95 million of 2026 headwind against 10-11% shipment growth. The second is simply the commodity base, which is large, inelastic and tracks insulin volumes rather than technology. Readers should forecast the two halves separately, and should prefer patients, pumps shipped and installed base — all of which Insulet, Tandem and Beta Bionics publish — over revenue, which is about to become a worse proxy for adoption than it already is.
reader_takeaways: Forecast the two halves separately. Pen needles, syringes and strips are about $5.00 billion growing 2-4.5%; pumps and pods are about $7.40 billion whose vendors grew 10.7% to 54% in FY2025. The published 7.9% describes neither.

Use patients, not dollars. Insulet, Tandem and Beta Bionics publish user counts with revenue — $4,500, about $3,383 and $2,865 per patient per year. Inverting the published total gives 1.6-2.6 million pump users, which you can sanity-check against clinical reality.

Note that the published pump segment is already full. Five disclosures account for 93.3% of it, leaving about $495 million for Roche, Sequel, Medtrum, Equil, SOOIL and all Chinese and Indian vendors combined.

Expect reported revenue to understate adoption from 2026. Tandem's guidance carries $85-95 million of pharmacy-channel headwind while shipments grow 10-11%, and Beta Bionics' pharmacy share of new starts went from high single digits to the high twenties in a year.

Remember that the biggest segment is invisible. Insulin pens are about 38% of the published market and neither Novo Nordisk nor Eli Lilly reports pen hardware separately from the insulin inside it, so that part of any estimate cannot be checked at all.
